title: Shelly — 22yo Hermann’s tortoise: not eating six weeks after hibernation
presentation: 22-year-old female Hermann’s tortoise, hibernated for four months in a garage, brought out six weeks ago and has eaten almost nothing since. Sunken eyes, and the owner has seen no urine passed.

stages.title: Assess the post-hibernation patient
stages.briefing: Weight 1.42 kg, down from 1.68 kg before hibernation. Eyes sunken, skin inelastic, mucous membranes tacky. Weak, minimal limb withdrawal. Mild periorbital swelling. Beak overgrown. No urine or urates passed in six weeks according to the owner. Hibernated at an unmonitored temperature in an unheated garage; no pre-hibernation health check.

options.label: No urine or urates passed in six weeks
options.detail: Renal failure or urate obstruction

options.label: Clinical dehydration with a 15% weight loss
options.detail: Fluid deficit that has to be corrected before anything else

options.label: Weakness with reduced limb withdrawal
options.detail: Systemic illness rather than simple slow warming

options.label: Overgrown beak
options.detail: A husbandry finding needing attention later

options.label: Unmonitored hibernation temperature
options.detail: Explains the situation but is not a clinical finding

stages.explanation: Post-hibernation anorexia is a presentation, not a diagnosis, and the question is always whether the tortoise is merely cold or genuinely ill. Six weeks without urine and a 15% weight loss answers it: this is renal and fluid failure, and the beak can wait. Anorexia beyond a fortnight after correct warming is never normal.

stages.title: Choose the tests
stages.briefing: The tortoise is warmed to its preferred body temperature and you can take blood from the jugular and radiograph.

options.label: Plasma uric acid, urea, calcium and phosphorus
options.detail: Renal function and the calcium-phosphorus product

options.label: Ionised calcium
options.detail: What the tissues actually see

options.label: Packed cell volume and total protein
options.detail: Hydration and protein status

options.label: Whole-body radiographs including a craniocaudal view
options.detail: Bladder stones, follicles, egg retention, bone density

options.label: Urinalysis if any urine can be obtained
options.detail: Concentration, crystals, cells

options.label: Mycoplasma agassizii PCR as the primary investigation
options.detail: Relevant with nasal discharge; the picture here is renal

options.label: Faecal culture as the first-line test
options.detail: Not the priority in a dehydrated anuric tortoise

stages.explanation: Chelonian renal disease is read from uric acid with the calcium and phosphorus alongside it: an inverted calcium-to-phosphorus ratio is the finding that separates renal failure from simple dehydration. Radiographs are cheap and answer two questions at once — retained eggs and bladder calculi both present as post-hibernation anorexia in a female of this age.

stages.title: Interpret the results
stages.briefing: Uric acid 1,180 µmol/L (ref 100–500). Urea 42 mmol/L (raised). Calcium 2.1 mmol/L, phosphorus 4.6 mmol/L, giving a Ca:P ratio of 0.46:1 (target above 1.5:1). Ionised calcium low. PCV 42% (raised, dehydration), total protein 68 g/L. Radiographs: no bladder calculi, no retained eggs, moderate loss of bone density with a thinned carapace. Small volume of urine obtained: urate-rich sediment, no bacteria.
stages.prompt: Which conclusions do these results support?

options.label: Renal failure with hyperuricaemia
options.detail: Uric acid 1,180 µmol/L with a raised urea

options.label: Inverted calcium-to-phosphorus ratio from phosphate retention
options.detail: Ca:P of 0.46:1

options.label: Dehydration is compounding the azotaemia
options.detail: A raised PCV with clinical dehydration

options.label: Retained eggs and bladder calculi are excluded
options.detail: Neither present on radiographs

options.label: Gout can be ruled out at this stage
options.detail: A uric acid this high risks visceral and articular gout, which has to be looked for

options.label: Bacterial cystitis explains the anuria
options.detail: No bacteria in the urine sediment

stages.explanation: The inverted Ca:P ratio is the number that turns "dehydrated tortoise" into "renal failure", because phosphate is retained when the kidney fails and it stays inverted after rehydration. Excluding eggs and stones on a radiograph is quick and prevents a missed surgical case. With uric acid this high, gout is a live risk rather than a settled question.

stages.title: Commit to a diagnosis
stages.briefing: Uric acid 1,180 µmol/L, urea 42 mmol/L, Ca:P 0.46:1, low ionised calcium, raised PCV with dehydration, no eggs or calculi, reduced bone density, six weeks of anorexia after an unmonitored hibernation.

options.label: Renal failure with hyperuricaemia and secondary calcium-phosphorus imbalance, on dehydration
options.detail: The kidney, its consequences and the fluid deficit

options.label: Simple post-hibernation dehydration
options.detail: Does not explain a Ca:P of 0.46:1 or a uric acid of 1,180 µmol/L

options.label: Follicular stasis
options.detail: No follicles or eggs on radiographs

options.label: Cystic calculus
options.detail: None visible radiographically

options.label: Nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism alone
options.detail: The bone changes are real but secondary to renal disease here

stages.explanation: The plan follows the order of the diagnosis: fluids first — warm baths and intravenous or intraosseous fluids rather than a syringe of food — then phosphate binding, nutritional support and a recheck of uric acid once rehydrated. The prognosis conversation is honest: renal damage in chelonians is often irreversible, and the next hibernation needs to be controlled and preceded by a health check.
